newsitem.title: CANADA: Some Winnipeggers to go home as flood recedes.
newsitem.headline: Some Winnipeggers to go home as flood recedes.

text.p: Pressure from the flooded Red River began to ease on Tuesday and officials told some of the families who had been forced to flee they could return home later this week.

About 1,200 of the 8,500 Canadian soldiers deployed to build dikes across Manitoba were ordered to pack up to start returning to their base as early as Wednesday to resume training for a peacekeeping mission in Bosnia.

"It reflects that things are stabilizing," Foreign Affairs Minister Lloyd Axworthy said. "The same kind of demands aren't there and the level of activity that's being called upon is now being reduced."
The first of the 8,800 evacuated Winnipeggers will be allowed back home starting on Thursday, with most allowed back in the next two weeks. The city is home to 650,000 people.

"We are announcing our plans to enable some city residents who have been evacuated to return safely to their homes," Winnipeg Mayor Susan Thompson said. "This can only happen once the threat of river flooding has passed and the safety of residents can be assured on a continuing basis."
The Red River level in downtown Winnipeg fell to 24.2 feet (7.4 meters) early on Tuesday after cresting last Thursday at 24.5 feet (7.5 metres), Thompson said.
More than 28,000 Canadians and 50,000 Americans have been forced from their homes by the worst flooding since 1852.
The floods devastated southern Manitoba and North Dakota, causing more than $1 billion in damage.

About 600 people were allowed to return to the towns of Letellier and Dominion City about 10 miles (17 km) north of the U.S.-Canada border on Tuesday. But flood waters were still too high to allow the 1,700 residents of Morris to return home. Morris is about 22 miles north (35 km) of Letellier.
"We're only allowing people to come in for emergency purposes, if they need medication and such," Royal Canadian Mounted Police Constable Mark Hustings said.
"We're urging people to be patient and wait a little bit longer. We should be allowing them to come back in the near future," Hustings added.
Another engineer regiment arrived in Winnipeg on Tuesday with heavy equipment to replace the redeployed battle group.

"I'd like to emphasize the rotation of these troops does not indicate a change in the commitment the Canadian Forces has to southern Manitobans," Major Rod Babiuk said. "I think the need is still great but it's the type of assets that we want to contribute to the solution that is slightly different."

Dikes in Canada's flood-ravaged Red River Valley were lashed on Monday by high winds and waves up to two feet (60 cm) high on the so-called "Red Sea," an expanse of floodwater twice the size of Hong Kong, which has submerged southern Manitoba.
More winds and some rain were forecast for the flood zone on Tuesday and on Wednesday. Defenses so far withstood the challenge without any major breaches, but 29 city homes had flooded.
